approachQuestion.prompt:
Worker and task assignment

Two arrays of equal length contain worker skill and task difficulty. Pair each worker with one task to minimize the sum of absolute differences; return that minimum. Any pairing is allowed. 0≤n≤200000; values within ±10^9; result fits signed 64-bit. Examples: workers=[1,10], tasks=[3,8]→4; [0,100] and [40,60]→80.

Do not modify either input. Values are opaque comparison keys; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside the stated model. Choose the most efficient valid method that returns the required result for every allowed input.
constraints: Inputs are read-only and must remain unchanged.
Only comparison-based ordering is allowed; hashing, radix, counting and bucket methods are outside this problem model.

options.text: Sort copies of both arrays in the same order and sum pairwise absolute differences.
options.feedback: Matching sorted ranks minimizes total absolute distance on a line.

options.text: For each worker, greedily pair it with the closest remaining task.
options.feedback: For workers [4,0] and tasks [3,10], choosing 3 for worker 4 first costs 1+10=11, while pairing 4→10 and 0→3 costs 6+3=9.

options.text: Pair arrays by their original indices.
options.feedback: Input order is arbitrary; [1,10] with [8,3] costs 14 rather than 4.

options.text: Enumerate all task permutations and retain the cheapest assignment.
options.feedback: Correct but factorially many assignments are unnecessary.

feedback.reason: Crossing two ordered assignments cannot improve the sum of absolute distances.
details: Sort copies of both arrays ascending, then sum absolute differences at matching indices.

Crossing two ordered assignments cannot improve the sum of absolute distances. Uncrossing repeatedly yields matching sorted ranks. This argument uses the one-dimensional absolute-distance objective, not an arbitrary assignment cost.
“Sort copies of both arrays in the same order and sum pairwise absolute differences.”: Matching sorted ranks minimizes total absolute distance on a line.
“For each worker, greedily pair it with the closest remaining task.”: For workers [4,0] and tasks [3,10], choosing 3 for worker 4 first costs 1+10=11, while pairing 4→10 and 0→3 costs 6+3=9.
“Pair arrays by their original indices.”: Input order is arbitrary; [1,10] with [8,3] costs 14 rather than 4.
“Enumerate all task permutations and retain the cheapest assignment.”: Correct but factorially many assignments are unnecessary.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed below, choose the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds. Count working copies, event/heap/visited storage and sort buffers; exclude the caller input and returned output. Comparisons and arithmetic take constant time; merge sort uses a linear buffer.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Two sorts dominate the rankwise distance sum.
details: Sorting both n-entry arrays gives 2*O(n log n), which remains O(n log n). Summing n rankwise distances adds O(n). Both copied inputs and reusable merge buffers are simultaneously bounded by a constant multiple of n, not n²; excluding the scalar result does not exclude these arrays.
